newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Weak bullion holds axe over SAfrica gold mine jobs.
newsitem.headline: Weak bullion holds axe over SAfrica gold mine jobs.

text.p: The bleak bullion price has raised an axe over South Africa's gold mines once again with Randfontein Estates Gold Mining Co Ltd the latest to fall victim to the threat of huge job cuts.
Reports on Tuesday said mining house JCI Ltd's Randfontein mine was considering retrenching up to two thirds of its 12,000-strong workforce.
This threat and recent warnings on job cuts from other mines is likely to cloud annual collective mine wage increase talks due to start in the next couple of weeks.
Randfontein is the latest of South Africa's gold mines to be haunted by the spectre of sacking and shaft closures in the face of a sickly bullion price.
Confirming that discussions were taking place on restructuring the mine's labour, JCI spokesman Marc Gonsalves said from London that a decision would be made within the next couple of days.
"The issues are not yet decided on and we can expect a report from the expert appointed to the union either today or tomorrow," Gonsalves said.
He declined to say how many jobs were on the line.
The local Business Report quoted the National Union of Mineworkers as saying the mine could retrench as many as 8,000, while the Business Day said 4,000 jobs could be cut.
March quarter gold results held only disappointment with the Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd, Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd and JCI Ltd stables all announcing sharp declines in profit.

Giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd announced last month that losses at the world's biggest gold mine, its Free State Consolidated Gold Mines Ltd, were unsustainable and the shafts might be forced to close.
Anglo's Vaal Reefs Exploration and Mining Co Ltd also warned of major job cuts.
The country's gold mining industry is plagued by falling production, declining ore grades and rising costs.
National output fell to 494.6 tonnes last year -- the lowest since the 1950's. Working costs have soared to an average 43,367 rand per kg of gold mined from 505 rand/kg in 1950.
Analysts said that 50 to 54 percent of working costs were due to labour and that in hard times labour was the area targetted first to lower costs.

"Randfontein is very much a sign of the times. The threat of job cuts has been there for some time. Jobs are on the line in order to work smarter. It's the nature of mining that when the gold price falls, pay (profitably mined) areas are reduced," said Dave Giese, analyst at Smith Borkhum Hare & Co.
Chamber of Mines statistics show that the number of workers employed on gold mines has fallen sharply to 342,439 by the end of 1996 from 534,255 in 1986.
South Africa's gold mines are the deepest in the world -- some nearing 5,000 metres -- and this makes them expensive to operate, with human labour the only feasible means to mine.
The bullion price's current shoddy show has cut the ground from under mines working tight margins.
To survive without aid from a dull gold price, these mines have to increase production or cut costs.
The threat of lost jobs is always there but analysts say working full calendar operations, ie. throughout holidays and weekends, could throw the industry a lifeline.

"It has a double impact. If you work more days it enables you to spread the overheads over more days and so reduce those costs. If you work more days it's more efficient without this stop-start business," Giese said.
